chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
title: Keeping a successful recorded solo; It's Got to Be This or That
summary: Stewart improvised solos differently each time but kept a solo that worked on a hit record, citing It's Got to Be This or That with Goodman.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: -- just about what he was going to do and especially after or rather, I might say, when I took my solos, I would say I would do my solos more or less improvisation, you know, because lots of times I'd never play the same, the solo, my solos the same way twice.

Of course, when we made recordings, if I made a solo, one solo or two, if the recording was a successful one, especially my solo, if it came out all right when I recorded and became very popular, I sort of kept the same solo that I made on the recording. I kept it in, you know, when we played on our gigs, the same number, I'd keep the same solo in that I recorded, because if the recording was successful.
So if it wasn't successful, you might play anything.
Yeah, because that was what I notice in a lot of guys. Sometimes if you don't -- if the audience requests that, if you don't play that, they might not even know it's the same tune.

That's right. That reminds me of the recording made with Benny Goodman with the big band back in the '40s, 'It's Got to Be This or That.' Any time that we performed that number in public, I played my same solo and did my same
clichés that I did on the recording because it was a very successful record. But you may have heard at the end of the record I -- say, 'It's got to be this or that.'
